evidence_quotes.quote: In this paper the role of infrastructure regulation in poverty reduction is investigated drawing on the published evidence. The conclusion is that the evidence is both patchy and sometimes contradictory.

The paper concludes by proposing a future research agenda aimed at improving our understanding of the ways in which infrastructure regulation impacts on poverty, with the objective of improving actual regulatory policy in developing economies.
This paper focuses on economic regulation and particularly the regulation of prices, outputs and service quality.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and poor consumers' access to infrastructure services in developing countries, explicitly including piped water, safe sanitation, community standpipes, private wells and sewerage connections alongside electricity and telecommunications.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 (examines regulatory, institutional and legal governance of infrastructure utilities) AND the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading (specifically discusses rule-type mechanisms directly governing service access and affordability, including concession exclusivity clauses banning community standpipes and private wells, non-recognition of the legality of dwellings in shanty towns, means-tested water and sanitation subsidies in Chile, automatic water rate adjustment rules in Ghana, statutory free basic water rights in South Africa and connection-charge instalment/social-tariff rules in Buenos Aires). However, the study still fails Criterion 3 because it is a non-empirical narrative review.
criterion_notes.c3: Unsystematic narrative literature overview and policy/research-agenda essay. Contains no primary empirical data, no secondary empirical dataset analysis and no systematic review methodology (no search strategy, databases, eligibility criteria, study selection process or structured synthesis). Excluded under E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Narratively discusses outcomes relevant to household water and sanitation connection, service exclusion and affordability cited from secondary literature, though no original empirical outcome data or systematic synthesis estimates are reported.
criterion_notes.c5: As a non-systematic narrative review and research-agenda paper, there is no empirical study design, no defined study population or sample and no systematic synthesis protocol.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English.

study_design: Unsystematic narrative literature review and research-agenda essay
country: Developing countries (global narrative overview citing examples from Latin America, Africa and Asia)
exposure: Infrastructure utility regulation and privatisation rules (including pricing/tariff rules, means-tested subsidies, concession exclusivity clauses, legal recognition of informal dwellings and regulatory capacity)
outcome: Poverty reduction and household access to and affordability of basic infrastructure services including water and sanitation (narratively cited from secondary literature)
rationale: Full text matches record metadata (Parker, Kirkpatrick & Figueira-Theodorakopoulou, 2008). Although the paper discusses water and sanitation service access and affordability (c1, c4) and examines rule-type regulatory and legal mechanisms directly governing service access under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of Criterion 2 (c2), it is an unsystematic narrative review of selected literature paired with a proposed future research agenda. It reports no primary or secondary empirical analysis of its own and employs no systematic review methods (no search strategy, inclusion criteria or systematic synthesis), failing Criterion 3 (exclude as E05 under both the narrow and plain Criterion 2 readings).
